One LAN, one cable for everyone

A local area network is one confined to an office, a floor or a building. The technology that prevailed is Ethernet (a DIX trademark: Digital, Intel and Xerox), which the IEEE standardized as 802.3.

In its original form it is a bus: a coax cable that all stations hang from. It is a peer to peer network (nobody has priority) and half-duplex.

1970 Aloha → 1979 Ethernet II → 1985 802.3 (10 Mbps) → 1995 Fast Ethernet → 1998 Gigabit → 2002 10 Gb. They all share the same frame format.
There is no central controller: access to the medium is distributed among all the stations.
Where Ethernet lives: MAC and LLC

Compared with OSI, Ethernet / 802.3 operates at the data link layer, which the IEEE splits into two sublayers:

  • LLC (Logical Link Control, 802.2): the upper one, common to all technologies.
  • MAC (Medium Access Control): the lower one, specific to each technology. Each committee standardized how the medium is accessed: 802.3 for Ethernet, 802.11 for Wi-Fi…
What changes between a wired and a wireless LAN is the MAC sublayer; the LLC stays the same.

When a station transmits (in baseband, with line codes such as Manchester), the signal occupies the whole medium and the others listen: this is a point-to-multipoint configuration.

Two needs follow from this:

  • A medium access control: how stations organize themselves to use the same cable.
  • Addressing: identifying sender and recipient. Each station compares the destination MAC with its own: if it matches it processes the frame, otherwise it discards it.

Before transmitting, the station listens to the medium. If it is free, it transmits; if it is busy, it waits until it becomes free.

Since Manchester has a transition in every bit interval, it is impossible for someone to be transmitting without it being noticed.

The frame propagates and everyone receives it. Each station checks the CRC and then the destination MAC.
CS = Carrier Sense (I listen) · MA = Multiple Access (there are several of us on the same medium).
B has a frame ready, but it detects a carrier on the cable. It will transmit only once the medium is free.

All of them run the same procedure, each on its own. It can happen that two see the medium free at the same instant and start together.

The signals interfere and nobody can understand anything: both transmissions must be repeated.

The collision is accounted for (this is the CD, Collision Detection): the station transmits and listens at the same time. If what it hears is not the same as what it sends, someone else is on the medium.
A collision is not a rare error: it is a normal part of how CSMA/CD works.

On detecting the collision, the standard calls for a JAMMING situation: the stations keep transmitting for a moment to make sure that all of them detect that a collision occurred.

Then each one increments its collision counter n and stops transmitting.

To avoid colliding again, each station randomly picks a number N between 0 and 2ⁿ − 1 and waits N · 2t before retrying.

With n = 1 there is a 50 % chance they pick the same value and collide again. Each collision raises n, the range doubles and the probability of a match drops.

The counter grows up to 10, but up to 16 attempts are made; if it still fails, the network is considered unreachable. With successful transmissions the counter goes back down.
The random delay is what breaks the tie: the more they collide, the further apart in time they spread.
The collision window and the 64 bytes

A thick coax segment is up to 500 m long (200 m for thin); with up to 4 repeaters it reaches 2.5 km. At 10 Mbps, by the time a station has transmitted 64 bytes, its signal has already filled the whole bus.

From that moment on nobody else will start (everyone listens first), so collisions can only happen within those first 64 bytes: the collision window.

If a frame were shorter, A would finish transmitting before the collision travels back to it, and it would not detect it. That is why the minimum is 64 bytes, and the PAD field fills in whatever is missing.
Minimum frame of 64 bytes = guarantee that the sender is still listening when the collision comes back.
A's signal takes time to travel the 2.5 km. D starts just before it arrives. The interference has to travel back to A while A is still transmitting: the 64 bytes guarantee that.

• I listen to the medium; if it is free, I transmit.
  • While transmitting I keep listening: if it differs, there was a collision.
  • Jam, add 1 to n and wait N · 2t with N random in 0…2ⁿ−1.
  • At most 16 attempts; n grows up to 10.
  • Minimum frame of 64 bytes to cover the collision window.

All of this holds as long as the medium is shared. In the next lesson we look inside the frame, and then at how hubs, bridges and switches gradually shrink (and eliminate) the problem.

The station transmits and listens in parallel; if what it hears is not the same as what it sends, someone else is on the medium.
After the third consecutive collision (n = 3), what range is N chosen from?
N is chosen at random between 0 and 2ⁿ − 1; with n = 3 that is 0…7, and the station waits N · 2t.
Why must an Ethernet frame be at least 64 bytes long?
So the sender keeps transmitting throughout the whole collision window
By 64 bytes the signal has filled the 2.5 km bus; if the frame were shorter, the collision would come back after the sender had stopped listening.
Which sublayer is common to all IEEE LAN technologies?
The LLC is the common upper sublayer; the MAC depends on each technology (802.3, 802.11…).
Peer to peer, half-duplex LAN with distributed medium access. Same frame format from 10 Mbps to 10 Gb.
